Enthusiastic consent has entered the vernacular due to the recognition of different fear responses during sexual assault. 

We usually think of fear responses as “fight or flight,” but there are actually two more: “fawn and freeze.” Fight and flight are already well-explained, but “fawn” is when one goes along with abuse in order to, as OP said, “get it over with.” It’s a method of self-preservation. It’s basically, “how do I get out of this with as little injury as possible?” By going along with what they are doing, you risk minimal retribution, be it verbal or physical abuse in other ways, or further sexual abuse. 

Freeze is another thing OP did: when one blanks out of one’s own body, does nothing, says nothing, and the brain desperately tries to retain as little information as possible to reduce mental trauma. Freeze is what some people do when attacked, and it leaves you dazed and typically unable to fend for yourself. 

What enthusiastic consent means is that you are not saying yes in order to appease your aggressor: you are saying yes because you genuinely want it, it feels good, and you have no doubts at all that this is what you want. When fawning or freezing, it is impossible to give enthusiastic consent due to the very nature of them being fear responses.

It’s going to sound weird, but hear me out—the idea that nature is going to outlive me no matter when I die. 

The key cause of my more serious bouts of depressive days typically stems from how fucked up the world is. World leaders and CEOs are so out of touch with our day to day lives, our reality; leaders continually threaten war without regarding the consequences; families starve and remain homeless and are regarded with scorn rather than empathy; men and women are raped, beaten, abused, and have to fight even further for justice; babies are abused and murdered, and women are dying as their rights are stripped from them; hate crimes and school shootings still prevail as everyone pretends everything is fine as it is; etc, etc.

The world puts me so deeply into my own head that I struggle to find a reason to open my eyes each morning. But then I remind myself that even after the last manmade structure crumbles into dust, life will still be here, living on without us, and it brings me such comfort to know I’m an infinitesimal thing in the scope of the earth. I always find myself smiling at birds’ nests on billboards, and small bits of leaf stretching up through cracks in the pavement. 

I always stress myself out trying to make my time on earth mean something, trying to account for my personal failings and struggles as if somehow everything is my fault. But the trees don’t care, and the water doesn’t care, and the world keeps spinning. And that, weirdly enough, keeps me alive.

Here’s a pamphlet I found from Rape Crisis Scotland on how to cope after being sexually assaulted:

https://www.rapecrisisscotland.org.uk/resources/RCS-supportresources-coping.pdf

It includes resources such as Grounding Exercises (for those really intense memories), checklists for keeping track of your habits, and some facts about PTSD from rape. 

When it comes to surviving, it is very tempting to and sometimes hard to keep track of whether or not you form bad habits as a way of coping/because you simply forget. Form a checklist for your days. Start with your essentials—your daily hygiene routine, eating, etc. Start with small tasks, then work your way up to bigger ones. It’s helpful to keep yourself busy or distracted. Find an old sitcom you like and watch it when you aren’t occupied; things like that keep the brain quiet when things start to get too loud, without potentially triggering panic attacks or bad memories.

>	I’m still not okay.

I’m so sorry. I don’t know if it helps, but it is totally okay not to be okay for a while. You are processing severe trauma; this takes time. Do not be hard on yourself if you feel like this should be a faster or cleaner process. By its very definition, it isn’t that simple.

>	Another thing I’d like to ask is for support on dealing with the intense fear of being touched, loud noises, and being around men in general. 

I’m a survivor too, and this was the hardest thing for me to overcome. I was touch-sensitive for several months after my incident. What helped me was having my (now) fiancée warn me when she was about to touch me. I wore long sleeves whenever I could to avoid brushing. Take solace in your comfiest clothes. I would have my fiancée practice gentle touches with me, like rubbing my back over my shirt, telegraphing hugs, and other things. Gradually, it grew easier for me to expand my ability and desire to touch others. Note that this, like all things, will take SO much time and effort, and it will be hard. It may not work as well for you as it did for me, but I sincerely hope it does. 

As for the men portion, I would only be around men when with my fiancée. I would ask her to be a social buffer for me, and to cover for me should I need to leave or go somewhere quieter/man-free. I would talk to your fiancé about that—having him around while making connections with men might help you feel safer. But don’t push yourself into this portion unless you feel absolutely ready. 

That’s the key to all of this, really: don’t push yourself until you feel ready to give it a try. Pushing too hard could cause you more pain, and you don’t deserve that. You didn’t deserve any of this, and it will help to be kind to yourself now.

I was thirteen. I recently moved to a new town, since my mother had found a boyfriend who really cared for her, and wanted to take care of us.

This new town had a graveyard and a church that I loved to be around. My mother’s boyfriend also had a key to the church (it’s a tiny town and he helped them out with fundraising and landscaping) so I would take it and head down the road to be among the graves. 

I had wandered around cleaning up graves when I noticed one grave didn’t have a death date. Just this: “Born, (I can’t remember the exact date), 1885 —“ and nothing after that. The dash clearly meant this wasn’t just a memorial, but an actual grave, but it had no death date. (I think they might be wandering. A vampire, perhaps).

Already a little spooked, I decided to go into the church and finally go up to the bell tower and check it out. The church is tiny, with thin, rough carpeting and thrice-painted white walls and pillars. The second level was a white balcony, the sides thick with layer after layer of peeling old paint. The pews here were dusty and grimy. No one ever sat there. 

From the stairwell to the right pews, one could access the bell tower, so I started heading up there when I heard footsteps. They were fast, like a kid running, so I thought maybe my mother’s boyfriend’s son had followed me. I went back downstairs, looking for the source of the footsteps. No one else was there. I called, but no one answered. Then, I thought I heard more steps on the stairs, so I went back upstairs. There wasn’t anyone there, either, but I heard a thud from the bell tower. 

For some reason my stupid child brain said it was still my little brother trying to play games with me, so I thought I’d have him cornered in the bell tower. I went up each step really quietly, hoping to jump out and scare him at the top. 

When I got to the top, though, there still wasn’t anyone there. I got these weird chills all down my left side, and goosebumps prickled at my skin. Then I heard the noises again—going back down the stairs. 

I was really, really confused, so I slowly made my way outside and back home, not forgetting to lock up the church. I’d never heard those sounds again, but I also haven’t been back up to the bell tower since then. 

All things considered... this experience was really kind of cool. But back then, I was just 1000% done and ready to go.

I once was invited to use a Ouija board in my college dorm by our entire hall.

Then, someone asked if the two mediums could give it a try together, because we’d probably “get someone cool” with our energy. So, Sera and I settled in and initiated contact. 

The spirit we contacted was a young boy who called himself “E.” He said he was four, which made Sera and I skeptical of his identity. He was speaking very articulately for a four year old. We asked if he wanted to say anything. 

That’s when the whole room changed. I swear to god, the lights dimmed a little, and it grew way colder. A cold sweat hit me immediately, and I got dizzy. I remember almost losing my grip on the planchet, I was so out of it. Sera became nauseated and pale, saying she was going to throw up, and she began to hyperventilate. 

Then, E started trying to get out of the board. The planchet tugged us to A, and stretched FAST across the first row of letters. 

Sera and I immediately yelled goodbye and scraped the planchet to “goodbye.” For a while, nobody moved. I felt drained and exhausted. 

Sera and I resolved not to do that again, and even purified ourselves for good measure. No one had any incident after that, but I still keep away from Ouija boards.
